method: Source review bound to the exact URL supplied in the curator DOCX. Only normal redirects and direct links exposed on the supplied pages were followed; no search-engine, title-search, or alternative-version discovery was used.
retrieval_policy: exact_supplied_url_first; direct redirects/PDF/full-text/primary links allowed; if curator requires a primary source that cannot be reached from the supplied page, defer rather than search

I12.title: If CERN can come up with the requisite billions, the Future Circular Collider is a go
I12.review_basis: The supplied Physics Today article was retrieved and directly links to CERN’s 2026 strategy site. Physics Today reports that the CERN Council adopted the update in May and selected FCC-ee as the next flagship, but the curator explicitly requires the CERN Council resolution itself; the directly linked CERN strategy resources did not expose a verifiable Council resolution in this environment.
I12.evidence_text: Physics Today reports that the CERN Council adopted the 2026 European Strategy for Particle Physics update in May, prioritising the Future Circular Collider after the High-Luminosity LHC. It also reports a 2028 funding decision point, possible participation by China, Japan, the United States and the European Union, and Chinese interest in joining the FCC if its domestic collider is not approved.

I13.title: Security of Supply and Interdependency: A New Approach to Strategic Autonomy and Indispensability
I13.review_basis: The supplied Europe Focus page was retrieved and cites the Bellais–Fiott IRIS paper in a footnote, but it does not provide a direct link to the IRIS paper. The curator explicitly says the record is cited secondhand and asks to locate the IRIS paper, so the exact-link-only manual path defers rather than searching for it.
I13.evidence_text: The supplied Europe Focus article discusses European defence-technology dependence, R&D underinvestment relative to the United States and China, US technological dominance, supply vulnerability and the need for faster European defence R&D and scaling. Its footnote cites Bellais and Fiott, Security of Supply and Interdependency, IRIS, 3 June 2026.

C11.title: European Biotech Act — Commission Staff Working Document C(2026) 3375 final (impact assessment)
C11.review_basis: The supplied Commission PDF was reviewed directly. It makes the R&I-geopolitical bridge explicit: the EU has a world-class biotechnology research base but trails competitors in translating research into development, deployment and manufacturing at scale; biotechnology is also treated as an economic-security technology with strategic-autonomy, technology-leakage and biosecurity implications.
C11.evidence_text: The Commission finds that the EU has a world-class scientific base in biotechnology but trails competitors in translating research into development, market deployment and manufacturing at scale. It identifies fragmented ecosystems, financing constraints and regulatory bottlenecks as causes of a widening global competitiveness gap. Biotechnology is also treated as critical to EU economic security, strategic autonomy and resilience, with technology-security, leakage and biosecurity risks. The proposed investment pilot with the EIB Group targets structural late-stage financing gaps and aims to mobilise private capital.
C11.display_claim: The EU’s world-class biotech science is not translating into development, market deployment and manufacturing at competitor scale; the Biotech Act pairs economic-security safeguards with investment and regulatory measures to close that conversion gap.
C11.matrix_basis: The empirical/problem-definition evidence is a conversion gap from strong EU research to weaker deployment, scale and financing versus competitors (C), while the proposed EIB-linked investment and strategic-project instruments are intended to create a home-scaling outcome (A).

C12.title: Innovation without borders
C12.authors: Ursel Baumann; Zöe Cullen; Ester Faia; Annalisa Ferrando; Ricardo Perez-Truglia; Judit Rariga
C12.review_basis: The supplied CEPR/VoxEU source was reviewed directly. It is substantive European innovation research, but its mechanism is intra-European AI diffusion and competition among euro-area firms. It does not substantively analyse an external geopolitical, economic-security or strategic-dependence mechanism, so Europe/innovation/foreign-firm language is not enough for pass 1.
C12.evidence_text: Using an experiment on 3,316 euro-area firms linked to the ECB SAFE survey, the authors find that AI adoption is driven primarily by competition pressure rather than informational spillovers. Firms underestimate competitors’ AI investment, including peers in other euro-area countries, and information about domestic competitors affects expected adoption more strongly than information about foreign peers. The policy discussion focuses on Single Market fragmentation, knowledge sharing and AI diffusion across Europe.

C13.title: Europe’s ungoverned space: Military AI and the autonomy that cannot be bought
C13.review_basis: The supplied CEPR/VoxEU column was reviewed directly. It explicitly links Europe’s defence AI capability gap to dependence on US-controlled frontier models and cloud infrastructure, unilateral US administrative authority, European industrial capacity and joint financing.
C13.evidence_text: The column argues that European defence ministries and intelligence services rely on AI and cloud infrastructure they do not control or independently audit. A June US export-control directive is used to show that access to a frontier model can be suspended by US administrative decision. The author estimates a ten-to-fifteen-year gap before Europe can negotiate as a peer and links that gap to sovereign cloud, defence-industrial scale and joint financing.
C13.display_claim: European defence and intelligence users remain dependent on US-controlled AI and cloud infrastructure that can be withdrawn by unilateral US decision; the source estimates a 10–15 year capability gap before Europe can negotiate as a peer.
C13.matrix_basis: The observed 2026 condition is rented frontier infrastructure: Europe accesses critical AI/cloud capability on terms ultimately controlled in the United States (I-C). The advocated long-run destination is European peer-level sovereign capability (A).

R14.title: Europe's regulatory double bind
R14.review_basis: The supplied CEPR/VoxEU column was reviewed directly. It links delayed AI Act implementation, missing standards/assessment capacity, dependence on foreign testing methodologies and US trade retaliation against EU digital enforcement to Europe’s ability to exercise regulatory sovereignty over frontier technology.
R14.evidence_text: The column documents a delay in the AI Act high-risk regime, incomplete harmonised standards and largely undesignated conformity-assessment bodies. It argues that absent European assessment capacity, compliance can default to methodologies developed in the systems’ jurisdictions of origin, mainly the United States. It also describes US Section 301 retaliation following EU digital-market enforcement and frames the combination as sovereignty costs both when Europe defers rules and when it enforces them.
R14.display_claim: Europe faces a regulatory double bind: delayed AI implementation and missing assessment capacity push operative rule-making outward, while enforcement against US technology firms can trigger trade retaliation.
R14.matrix_basis: The immediate mechanism is implementation delay and institutional inability to operationalise adopted rules (R-D), while the source’s explicit sovereignty claim is that operative authority migrates to external methodologies and actors (R-C).

W15.title: German prosecutors allege China-linked collection targeting university aerospace, computer-science and AI researchers
W15.review_basis: The supplied Euronews page was retrieved and reports detailed allegations attributed to the German federal prosecution service, including contacts with researchers in aerospace engineering, computer science and AI. The curator explicitly marks the Federal Prosecutor release as verification outstanding; no direct primary link is exposed on the supplied page, so the exact-link path defers.
W15.evidence_text: Euronews reports that German prosecutors arrested a married couple suspected of working for a Chinese intelligence service and alleged they had established contacts with academics at German universities and research institutions in aerospace engineering, computer science and artificial intelligence. Some scientists were allegedly induced to travel to China for paid lectures that were delivered to employees of state-owned arms manufacturers.

W16.title: AI researcher with a prior European Space Agency placement arrested at NATO’s SHAPE on suspicion of espionage
W16.authors: Jesse Pinster; Follow the Money partners
W16.source: Follow the Money / Belgian Federal Prosecutor
W16.review_basis: The supplied Follow the Money article directly links to the Belgian Federal Prosecutor release. The official release verifies the arrest of a Canadian national of Chinese origin who was interning at SHAPE on suspicion of espionage for a third country; the supplied article independently reports that the suspect is an AI researcher who previously worked at ESA’s research centre and other international organisations.
W16.evidence_text: The Belgian Federal Prosecutor states that a Canadian national of Chinese origin, then an intern at NATO’s SHAPE headquarters in Mons, was placed under arrest on suspicion of espionage for a third country and participation in a criminal organisation. Follow the Money identifies the suspect as an artificial-intelligence researcher and reports a prior placement at the European Space Agency research centre in Italy, making the case a research-security signal about temporary access and screening rather than nationality alone.
W16.display_claim: A suspected-espionage case at NATO’s SHAPE involved an AI researcher with prior European Space Agency (ESA) research-centre experience, highlighting temporary research and technical access as a security-screening channel beyond nationality alone.
W16.matrix_basis: The event is evidence of the security pressure behind restrictions and screening around European research/talent access, matching the Knowledge-row closed-lab mechanism (K-B).

W17.title: Helsing and Quantum Systems raise $1.8bn and $1.2bn mega-rounds to scale European defence AI and autonomous systems
W17.review_basis: The supplied Defense News page directly links to primary company releases from Helsing and Quantum Systems. Those releases verify $1.8bn and $1.2bn financing rounds, European defence-AI/autonomy scale-up and, for Helsing, continued predominantly European ownership. The manual record’s separate Stark claim is not needed for admission and is not used as reviewed evidence here.
W17.evidence_text: Helsing announced a $1.8 billion Series E at an $18 billion valuation, with investors including US and other global institutions, while stating that the company remained predominantly European-owned and would use the investment to accelerate defence AI platforms. Quantum Systems announced a $1.2 billion Series D to scale software-defined autonomous systems in Europe and next-generation sovereign European defence capabilities. Together the directly linked releases show very large growth-stage capital reaching European defence-technology firms without an observed relocation from Europe.
W17.display_claim: Helsing and Quantum Systems raised $1.8bn and $1.2bn to scale European defence AI/autonomy, showing that late-stage capital can reach European firms in this sector even when a substantial share of the capital is global.
W17.matrix_basis: The observed firms remain European and are using mega-rounds to scale production and capability, which fits Home champion (C-A); the curator’s C-C concern about foreign capital remains preserved as a competing interpretation but is not an observed foreign exit.

W18.title: EU digital enforcement and US Section 301 retaliation sequence
W18.review_basis: The supplied URL is the R14 CEPR/VoxEU synthesis, as the curator notes. It names Commission, Reuters and USTR references for the July enforcement/retaliation sequence but does not expose direct links for the key 23–24 July primary/current-event references. Under the exact-link-only rule the weak signal is deferred rather than reconstructed through search.
W18.evidence_text: The supplied CEPR/VoxEU column describes a 23 July European Commission Google DMA fine and a 24 July announcement of a US Section 301 investigation, framing the sequence as a cost of European digital enforcement. Because the manual record explicitly requires direct Commission, Reuters and USTR verification, the synthesis is retained as secondary evidence only.

W19.title: Hungary election removes a major EU veto player; institutional consequences remain context for the radar window
W19.review_basis: The supplied Atlantic Council article is dated 13 April 2026, before the radar corpus start. It discusses the election result and expected effects on Hungarian veto behaviour, but the separately claimed 9 May government formation is not established by the supplied page. The item is therefore retained as context rather than admitted as an in-window weak signal.
W19.evidence_text: The Atlantic Council analysis says Tisza won a two-thirds parliamentary majority and expects a Magyar-led government to remove or reduce Hungary’s habitual obstruction on EU dossiers such as Ukraine support, the next multiannual budget and further integration. The source itself was published on 13 April 2026, outside the radar’s primary window.
